2026 kitchen gift guide: Essential cooking gear for chefs of every level

📅 2022-11-16  |  Read Source →

Updated Nov 11, 2026 10:48 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

You don’t have to be great at cooking to enjoy it. Having the right gear really helps, though, and that creates a wellspring of great gifting opportunities. The HORL3 Cruise holds a knife against a magnet at a fixed 15- or 20-degree angle while a diamond disc rolls along the edge. The ThermoWorks Thermapen Nano gets a reading in about 0.4 seconds, so you can stop guessing when a roast is done. The Challenger Bread Pan traps steam under a tall cast-iron lid, the same trick bakeries pull off with steam-injected ovens. Every pick below works on that principle, from a $16 three-pack of Swiss peelers to a $750 Ankarsrum stand mixer whose bowl spins on top of the motor instead of under a beater.

There are 65 gifts here, grouped by category. Jump to: precision and measurement, knives and sharpening, pans and cookware, coffee, tea and drinks, baking and from scratch, countertop appliances, prep and storage, pantry and stocking stuffers.

Seasoning a thick steak with a typical pepper grinder takes a lot of twisting. The MÄNNKITCHEN Pepper Cannon uses hardened high-carbon stainless steel burrs spinning on a drive shaft supported by two bearings inside a body milled from a solid block of anodized aluminum. MÄNNKITCHEN claims 10 times the output of top-rated mills, which it describes as seven cranks instead of 70. You set the grind from 8 to 60+ mesh with an adjuster on the base that clicks into spring-loaded detents. The hopper holds half a cup of peppercorns, and a removable cup underneath catches up to a third of a cup of ground pepper, which is handy when a rub calls for a measured amount.

A big mixing bowl tends to hide a kitchen scale’s display right when you need to read it. On the OXO Good Grips 11 lb Stainless Steel Food Scale with Pull-Out Display, the readout sits on a tray that slides out from the base, clear of whatever’s on the platform, then tucks back in for storage. It weighs up to 11 pounds (5 kilograms), and a meter on the display shows how much capacity you have left as you add ingredients. The display has an optional backlight, and the stainless steel platform lifts off so you can wash it by hand.

Sous vide cooking holds a water bath at the exact temperature you want your food to finish at, so a steak can sit in it and stay medium-rare instead of drifting toward well-done. The Anova Precision Cooker 3.0 heats that bath with an 1,100-watt element and circulates 8 liters of water per minute, and Anova rates it to hold within 0.2°F anywhere from 32°F to 197°F. A two-line touchscreen on the cooker shows time and temperature, and dual-band Wi-Fi lets you start or check a cook from your phone. Anova gives it an IPX7 water-resistance rating, and the clamp adjusts and detaches to fit different pots.

ThermoWorks has closed out the Thermapen One, and the Thermapen Nano took its place this year. ThermoWorks rates the Nano’s fixed thermocouple probe for a full reading in 0.4 seconds and accuracy within 0.5°F between -4°F and 248°F, a window that covers everything from rare beef to pulled pork. Two magnets built into the body let it ride on the side of the fridge or range hood, and the display rotates a full 360 degrees, so the numbers read right-side up whichever hand you hold it in. It’s IP67 rated, runs roughly 1,000 hours on one AAA battery, and comes with a five-year warranty and a NIST-traceable calibration certificate.

A fast thermocouple thermometer doesn’t have to cost triple digits. TempPro, the brand formerly known as ThermoPro, builds a thermocouple sensor into the TempSwift Pro TP622 and rates it for a 0.1-second response time and accuracy within 0.5°F across -58°F to 572°F. That high end reaches past meat into frying oil and candy-making territory. The backlit display auto-rotates 180 degrees for left- or right-handed use, and the thermometer wakes up when you lift it and goes to sleep after 90 seconds of sitting still. It carries an IP65 water-resistance rating and runs on a single AAA battery.

The Combustion Predictive Thermometer (2nd Gen) is built around the question people actually ask during a roast: how much longer? Its probe carries eight sensors along its length, so the app can show the core, the surface and the air temperature around the food at the same time. Combustion’s prediction engine uses that heat-flow data to estimate the time remaining, and a feature it calls TrueCore reports the lowest internal reading even if you didn’t hit the center. Combustion rates the upper half of the probe to 900°F, so it can stay in a roast under the broiler or on the grill. Bluetooth reaches more than 330 feet in open air, and Wi-Fi requires a separate booster accessory.

Freehand sharpening is hard mostly because holding a steady angle is hard. The HORL3 Cruise takes that job off your hands: a magnetic block holds the knife at either 15 or 20 degrees, and you roll a wheel with a diamond disc back and forth along the edge. The other end of the roller carries a stainless steel honing disc to straighten and refine the edge you just ground. The Cruise’s body is made from ocean-bound recycled plastic, and HORL builds it in Germany. If the person you’re shopping for would rather have wood on the counter, the $179 HORL3 uses an oak or walnut body and swaps in an interchangeable ceramic disc.

STEELPORT forges its 8-inch Chef Knife from a single billet of American 52100 carbon steel in Portland, Oregon, then heat treats the edge and spine differently. The company says the edge ends up around 65 HRC, hard enough to take and hold a fine edge, while the spine stays below 30 HRC so the blade as a whole is less brittle. The handle is resin-stabilized Oregon bigleaf maple burl, and a magnetic walnut sheath comes in the box. Carbon steel picks up a patina and can rust, so wipe it dry after every wash. STEELPORT covers the knife with a lifetime warranty and sharpens it free for as long as you own it.

A knife that suddenly feels dull often has an edge that’s just rolled over, and a few passes on a honing rod push it back into line between real sharpenings. STEELPORT’s 12-Inch Oval Ceramic Honing Rod does that with a fine-grit ceramic surface over a steel core. The oval cross-section is there for contact, and STEELPORT says it puts more of the blade against the rod than a round one does. The rod measures 17 inches overall with a 5-inch contoured walnut handle and a finger guard, and it weighs 12 ounces. Ceramic can crack if it hits a tile floor, so give it a hook or its own drawer slot.

Shun builds the Classic 8-Inch Chef’s Knife around a VG-MAX steel core clad in 34 layers of stainless Damascus on each side, which is where the rippled pattern on the blade comes from. The core is hardened to 60-61 on the Rockwell scale and hand-sharpened to about 16 degrees per side, a fine edge that slices through onions and herbs cleanly. The full-tang blade sits in a D-shaped black PakkaWood handle, and the whole knife weighs 7.5 ounces. Shun makes it in Seki, Japan. A hard, thin edge like this one is happiest on a wood or plastic board, and it shouldn’t go anywhere near bones or frozen food.

Softer stainless steel is quicker to bring back to a sharp edge, and that’s part of the appeal of the Made In 8-Inch Chef Knife. It’s fully forged in Thiers, France, from nitrogen-treated X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58+ HRC, so a few passes on a whetstone or rolling sharpener refresh it. Made In grinds the edge asymmetrically, with a 14-degree primary bevel on one side and a 4-degree polishing bevel on the other, for 18 degrees total. The blade actually measures 8.5 inches and the knife weighs 7 ounces. If you order directly from Made In, the company will engrave it for $30 more, but engraved knives can’t be returned.

Someone outfitting a first real kitchen needs a handful of good knives more than a block with 15 slots. The Cangshan N1 Series 6-Piece Knife Block Set forges its blades from German X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58 HRC, a steel that’s easy to touch up at home. The N1’s signature is its patented all-metal hollow handle, which runs straight out of the blade, so there are no wood or plastic scales to crack or loosen. Cangshan sells the set under more than one model number, so check the knife list on the listing before you order.

Tojiro has renamed its long-running DP line to Classic, but the F-808 210mm gyuto itself didn’t change. It’s a san mai blade, with a VG10 stainless core hardened to about 60 HRC sandwiched between softer stainless outer layers that add toughness around the hard cutting steel. The 50/50 double-bevel edge suits right- and left-handed cooks equally, and the Western-style handle has a full tang, a stainless bolster and three rivets, so it’ll feel familiar to anyone coming from a German knife. Tojiro makes it in Tsubame-Sanjo, Japan. The edge measures 212 millimeters and the knife weighs 7.2 ounces.

Learning to sharpen on a stone starts with two grits, and the King KW-65 puts both on one block. The 1000-grit side does the sharpening and raises a fresh edge, then the 6000-grit side polishes it. It’s a soaking stone, so you submerge it for a couple of minutes before you start and keep it wet while you work. The muddy slurry that builds up on the surface helps it cut, so leave it there rather than rinsing it away mid-session. The stone measures about 7.3 by 2.5 by 1 inches, sits in an included plastic stand, and is made in Japan.

The deep, 6-quart sauté pan at the center of the All-Clad NS Pro Ceramic Nonstick VIP comes with a steamer insert, a roasting rack and a tempered glass lid, so one piece of cookware can sear and steam on the stovetop or roast in the oven. The body is hard-anodized recycled aluminum, and a stainless steel base bonded underneath makes it work on induction burners. The ceramic nonstick interior is oven-safe to 450°F, though the lid tops out at 350°F and the pan can’t go under the broiler. Wash it by hand, and know that All-Clad’s warranty on this pan runs one year.

Carbon steel seasons and sears like cast iron, and it heats up and cools down faster when you adjust the burner. Made In’s Seasoned Carbon Steel Frying Pan arrives pre-seasoned with shea nut and coconut oils, so you can start cooking in it sooner than you could with a bare pan. The 12-inch size weighs 4.31 pounds, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2.25-inch sides. Made In builds it in Sweden, rates it for heat up to 1,200°F, and says it works on induction and over an open fire. The hollow stainless handle is designed to stay cool, and the pan should be washed by hand and dried right away.

Smithey is better known for cast iron, but its Deep Farmhouse Skillet is hand-forged carbon steel, made in Charleston, South Carolina. It’s about 12 inches across the top and 2 inches deep, which leaves room for a pan sauce or a shallow fry, and the cooking surface measures about 9.5 inches. Long handles on both sides stretch it to almost 21 inches end to end, so you can carry all 6 pounds of it to the table with two hands. Smithey lists it for use on gas, induction, electric and open fire.

Smithey’s 7.25 QT Dutch Oven skips enamel entirely. It’s bare cast iron with a fully polished interior, pre-seasoned with grapeseed oil, so it builds up seasoning the same way a skillet does and there’s no enamel coating to chip. The domed lid has drip channels on its underside that send condensation back down onto the food during a long braise. Expect some heft, since it weighs about 17.3 pounds with the lid. Smithey makes it in the US and backs it with a lifetime guarantee. Bare iron doesn’t love long simmers in tomato or wine, so save those braises for an enameled pot or keep them short.

Old cast iron is prized for its smooth, machined cooking surfaces, and Lancaster Cast Iron’s No. 8 Skillet brings that finish to a new pan. The cooking surface is polished smooth, then pre-seasoned with two layers of grapeseed oil at the company’s shop in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The No. 8 measures 10.5 inches across the top, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2-inch walls, and it weighs about 4 pounds. Polished iron starts out slick, and it gets slicker as layers of seasoning build up with every cook.

A saucier’s rounded bottom leaves no corners for a whisk or spatula to miss, which makes it the pan for custard and polenta and anything else that likes to scorch where the wall meets the floor. The Misen 3 QT Stainless Steel Saucier is 5-ply, with aluminum layers sandwiched inside stainless steel to spread heat across the base, and the walls are 3 millimeters thick. It measures about 9 inches across, comes with a lid, works on induction, and is oven-safe to 800°F. Misen backs it with a lifetime warranty against defects.

Kuhn Rikon’s 4th Burner Pot is tall and narrow, 5.5 inches across and holding 12 cups, so it fits on the small back burner while bigger pans take the front of the stove. That makes it handy for a couple of servings of pasta or a batch of blanched green beans. The glass lid has two built-in strainers and a pour spout, which lets you drain without hauling out a colander, and a removable basket inside handles steaming. Interior measurement marks save you a measuring cup, the silicone handles stay cool, and the stainless pot works on induction.

Microwave cooking goes better when steam is managed, and that’s the idea behind the Anyday 8-Piece Glass Round Dish Set. Each borosilicate glass dish gets a tempered glass lid with a silicone vent and gasket that let steam build and escape while the food cooks. Anyday says the stainless steel rim on each lid is microwave-safe as long as the dish sits at least an inch from the microwave’s walls. The set includes four dishes: two 4-cup sizes, one shallow and one deep, plus a 7-cup and an 8-cup. The bowls can go in the oven up to 500°F, so leftovers can get a crisp finish after they reheat.

Green tea scorches at a full boil, and pour-over coffee likes water a few degrees below it. The Fellow Corvo EKG Pro lets you dial in anywhere from 104 to 212 degrees Fahrenheit, then hold that temperature for 15 to 60 minutes so the second cup is as hot as the first. It also has an altitude setting, scheduling, and a pre-boil sanitize mode. The 0.9-liter body is 304 stainless steel. Fellow says the Wi-Fi only handles firmware updates, so you’ll still set the temperature on the kettle itself rather than from your phone.

Uneven grounds make uneven coffee, because the fine bits over-extract while the big chunks barely give up any flavor. The Fellow Ode Brew Grinder Gen 2 uses 64 mm stainless steel flat burrs, which cut a more uniform particle than the blade grinders most people start with. You get 11 settings split into 31 steps, a 100-gram capacity, and anti-static tech to keep grounds from clinging to the catch cup. Fellow built it for drip, pour-over, French press, and cold brew. It isn’t designed for espresso, so skip it for anyone pulling shots at home.

A coffee maker can only brew as well as its water temperature allows. The Moccamaster KBGV Select, handmade in the Netherlands, heats water quickly to brewing temperature with a copper boiling element, and the hot plate runs on its own separate element so it doesn’t cook the coffee sitting in the carafe. A switch on the brew basket adjusts the flow for a full 10-cup pot or a half batch, which keeps small batches from coming out thin. It carries the Specialty Coffee Association’s certification and a five-year warranty.

Most of the frustration of home espresso comes from dosing and grinding by feel. The Ninja Luxe Café Premier handles both: it has a conical burr grinder with 25 settings and a built-in scale that weighs the grounds for you, so each shot starts from a consistent dose. The Dual Froth System has four hands-free presets for steamed or frothed milk, and the machine also makes drip-style coffee and cold brew. It suits someone who wants café drinks without learning to tamp and time shots by eye.

Most countertop carbonators tell you to fizz plain water and add flavor afterward, because carbonating juice or wine tends to foam over. The Drinkmate OmniFizz gets around that with what the company calls its Fizz Infuser cap, which releases pressure gradually so you can carbonate cold drinks other than water. It runs on standard 60-liter CO2 cylinders, and Drinkmate sells it alone or in bundles with extra cylinders. Check the bundles before buying, since the kits with more cylinders were sometimes cheaper than the smaller ones in early November.

Matcha powder starts losing its color and flavor once it’s ground, which is why the Cuzen Matcha Maker grinds whole tea leaves on demand. Its hopper holds up to 20 grams of leaf, and the machine mills it, then mixes it with water in the cup using a magnetic whisk. You can pick a 1-, 1.5-, or 2-gram shot depending on how strong you like it, and there’s a grind-only mode for baking or lattes. The Starter Kit comes with 4-gram samples of three Cuzen leaf blends and a brush for cleaning the mill.

Pod-based cocktail machines lock you into one company’s drinks. The Barsys 360 uses whatever you put in it: six 750-milliliter canisters hold your own spirits, juices, and syrups, and a Bluetooth app tells the machine how much of each to pour through the spouts over the glass. It doesn’t shake or stir, so plan on finishing drinks the old-fashioned way. It also runs on USB-C power and weighs about 10 pounds empty, which makes it easier than you’d expect to move from the counter to a party table.

Nugget ice, the soft, chewable kind, is made by compressing ice flakes rather than freezing cubes in a tray. The GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro does that on your counter, and Govee rates it for up to 60 pounds a day, with the first batch ready in about six minutes. A 4.9-liter side tank supplements the 2.2-liter main reservoir so you refill less often, and it has two self-cleaning cycles. You can also check on it or start it from the Govee app or by voice with Alexa or Google.

Centrifugal juicers spin produce against a fast blade, while slow juicers like the Hurom H310 Easy Clean press it with a turning screw at roughly 45 rotations per minute. Hurom’s version has a self-feeding hopper with a 50-millimeter chute that the company says fits whole apples, which cuts down on prep. Hurom backs the 150-watt motor with a 10-year warranty and covers the other parts for two years.

Boxed wine stays fresh longer than an open bottle, but the cardboard box is nobody’s idea of a centerpiece. The Boxxle Box Wine Dispenser is a stainless steel and ABS plastic housing for the bag inside a standard box. According to Boxxle, it lifts the bag so the spout sits above your glass and presses on the bag as it empties, so you can keep pouring until the last glass.

Fresh pasta dough needs to be rolled thin and evenly, and doing it with a rolling pin takes practice most people don’t have. The Marcato Atlas 150 is a hand-cranked roller with a 10-position thickness dial, so you can step the dough down a little at a time until it’s thin enough for lasagna sheets. The rollers are anodized aluminum, and the body is chrome-plated steel made in Italy. The version sold in the US includes fettuccine and spaghetti cutters, so you can go from sheet to noodles without buying attachments.

Most stand mixers drive a beater from above. The Ankarsrum Assistent Original flips that: its motor sits in the base and spins the 7-liter stainless steel bowl itself, while a dough hook or roller stays put. That design is why Ankarsrum says it can knead up to 5 kilograms of dough, a load that would stall a lot of tilt-head mixers. The Essential Package comes with a dough roller, dough knife, dough hook, spatula, and a proofing lid. Ankarsrum covers the base with a seven-year warranty, though accessories aren’t included.

Bread machines have a reputation for pale, unevenly baked tops. The Zojirushi Home Bakery Virtuoso Plus adds a heater in the lid to go with the usual one underneath, so the top of the loaf browns along with the sides. It bakes a 2-pound loaf and uses two kneading blades, which helps it work a full 2-pound batch of dough evenly.

Sourdough gets its crackly crust from steam trapped around the loaf early in the bake, which is why so many bakers use a Dutch oven. The Challenger Bread Pan rearranges that idea: you set the dough on a shallow cast-iron base and lower a tall domed lid over it, so you’re not dropping a floppy loaf into a deep, 500-degree pot. It weighs 20 pounds, is made in the USA, and is rated to 500 degrees Fahrenheit. Its 15.5-by-10.5-inch footprint fits oblong batards as well as round boules.

HexClad’s hybrid surface finally made the jump from frying pans to the oven. The HexClad Hybrid Baking Sheets use the same pattern of raised stainless steel hexagons with nonstick valleys in between, built over 2.5-millimeter tri-ply with an aluminum core. HexClad says the ceramic coating is free of PFAS and rates the sheets for oven temperatures up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit. They’re sold in two-packs in small and medium sizes, and the medium sheet measures 10 by 15 inches. HexClad says they’re dishwasher-safe but recommends washing them by hand.

Detroit-style pizza owes its crunchy, cheese-crisped edges to a deep rectangular pan that conducts heat fast. The LloydPans 10×14 Detroit-Style Pizza Pan is 2.5 inches deep and made from 14-gauge anodized aluminum in Spokane Valley, Washington. Its Pre-Seasoned Tuff-Kote finish means you can skip seasoning and use metal utensils on it, according to LloydPans. Spread the cheese all the way to the edges so it melts down the sides and fries against the metal.

Stretching pizza dough on a countertop usually ends with flour everywhere. The Gozney Pizza Prep Board has raised edges that keep the flour on the board and a catch tray at the back where you can sweep extra flour and reuse it. Its textured surface holds a thin, even coating of flour, which Gozney says works better than wood, steel, or marble at keeping dough from sticking and tearing on its way to the peel. A bench hook keeps it from sliding, and size markings go up to 16 inches. It’s 22 by 21.5 inches, so check counter space first.

Neapolitan pizza wants a stone near 850 degrees Fahrenheit, a temperature home ovens don’t reach. The Ooni Volt 2, successor to the Volt 12, gets there on a standard 120-volt outlet in about 20 minutes, according to Ooni. Inside is a 10-millimeter cordierite stone sized for 12-inch pizzas, and Ooni’s Pizza Intelligence system shifts power between the heating elements as you cook. Presets cover Neapolitan, thin and crispy, and pan pizza. At about 39 pounds, it’s heavy enough that you’ll want to give it a permanent spot.

Chef Nancy Silverton started with a quarter sheet pan when she helped Made In design this dish, then stretched it longer and wider. The Made In Porcelain Baking Slab is a 9-by-13-inch French porcelain dish fired three times in the Loire Valley, with a lower profile than a typical casserole so roasted vegetables and gratins get more browning. It’s oven-safe to 650 degrees Fahrenheit and microwave-safe, and it weighs 3.8 pounds. Made In’s care guide says it can go in the dishwasher, though the company’s FAQ recommends hand washing.

Nik Sharma’s newest book builds its 100 recipes around the science of flavor, explaining why each technique works. Fundamentals of Flavor: 100 Recipes for the Science of Better Cooking came out from Chronicle Books in September 2026. It’s a good fit for the cook who keeps asking why a recipe calls for a specific step, and wants the answer along with dinner.

Caramelized Onion &amp; Goat Cheese Bites

📅 2022-11-08  |  Read Source →

With just a few simple ingredients, puff pastry, caramelized onions, and goat cheese come together to make one of the easiest and best holiday appetizers. The bites will have you coming back for seconds and thirds (it’s worth making a double batch for a big crowd). These are a great finger food to pile onto a platter for your Thanksgiving dinner or holiday celebration. You’ll be amazed at how easy they are to make and how impressed people will be when they eat one.

Crock-Pot Green Bean Casserole

📅 2022-10-13  |  Read Source →

Your oven this Thanksgiving is probably booked solid with baking turkey and sweet potatoes, so to lighten the load, this green bean casserole can be made entirely in a slow cooker. The cream of mushroom soup, milk, and spices get whisked really well in the slow cooker first to avoid pulling out a separate bowl, then the green beans get folded in after. Depending on your schedule, you can choose your cook time (2 1/2 hours on high or 5 to 6 hours on low). Bonus, the warm setting on your slow cooker will keep the casserole at perfect serving temperature until you’re ready to eat!

Grab your 6-quart slow cooker and whisk together the soup, milk, onion powder, and a teaspoon of pepper right inside. Next, stir in the green beans and a cup of fried onions. Pop the lid on and cook. Set it to High for 2 to 2 1/2 hours, or Low for 5 to 6 hours, depending on your schedule.

While that’s cooking, grab a medium skillet and toast the rest of the fried onions over medium-high heat. Give them a stir now and then, and they’ll be perfectly golden brown in about 3 minutes.

Once the casserole is ready, season it with a little salt and pepper to taste.

Then sprinkle those toasted fried onions on top for the perfect finish.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Store leftover green beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. When ready to serve, reheat in the microwave or in a saucepan over low heat.

Best Electric Ride-On Cars for Kids

📅 2022-10-06  |  Read Source →

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

If you’re shopping for a child obsessed with everything automotive, a ride-on electric car makes a great gift. Our staff dads pick their favorites.

This article was updated in November 2026 with new products and information.

For kids with even the slightest interest in cars, trucks, tractors, or fire engines, an electric ride-on is a gift that can transform a childhood. Yes, they can be pricey—but at this point, you might pay gold to have some quiet time in the house. That’s what these ride-on cars can provide: hours of outdoor fun that can help build fine motor skills, gross motor skills, and a real sense of freedom.

From rugged UTVs, dump trucks, realistic sports cars, pickup trucks, fire engines, and even mini motorcycles, there’s an electric ride-on to match every young driver’s interest. We’ve rounded up the best electric ride-on cars for kids that are available today to help you choose the right one.

We’ve even tested some of these with our own families, while others have been rounded up and assessed based on their descriptions and reviews. Either way, here’s a list of the most popular models that feature plenty of neighborhood-cruising fun.

This beautiful Bentley comes in a classy, pearly white. It features working LED headlights, functional scissor doors, a high/low speed switch, and realistic engine noises.

Like all the best electric cars for kids, it also sports a remote control for parents to keep their little racer from driving away. With a top speed of about 3 mph, it offers a full hour of playtime, depending on speed and terrain. Recommended for kids three to six years of age, it has a weight capacity of 66 pounds.

This officially licensed G63 comes with tons of authentic touches, including exhaust pipes, body-detail decals, and opening doors that lock from the outside for safety. The seatbelt and soft-start design prevent kids from being startled by sudden acceleration. The spring suspension ensures smooth rides.

We really like that the side window piece can be removed as kids grow, extending the usable life of the toy.

This is an officially licensed Chevrolet Silverado Trail Boss ride-on pickup truck. It features LED lights, startup sounds, and openable doors, as well as forward/reverse gears and Bluetooth connectivity. The maximum weight capacity is 66 pounds, suitable for ages 37–72 months.

The Peg Perego John Deere Ground Force Tractor is a rugged 12-volt ride-on that brings farm fun to life for kids aged three to seven. With two speeds (2.3 and 4.5 mph), reverse, and automatic brakes, it’s easy for young drivers to operate safely, and parents can use the 4.5-mph lockout for beginners. Farm-style wheels provide traction on grass, dirt, and pavement, and the extra-large stake-side trailer is perfect for hauling toys and treasures around the yard.

For added fun, the tractor features a working FM radio, an adjustable seat, and flip-up armrests for comfort as kids grow. Built to handle plenty of outdoor play, it includes a rechargeable 12-volt battery and charger. Made in the U.S.A., this tractor combines the classic green-and-yellow John Deere style with kid-friendly durability and design for hours of outdoor adventure.

Little adventure seekers will get a kick out of this replica Jeep, with its LED headlights, lockable doors, grid windshield, and off-road tires. It includes a parent remote, a spring suspension, and a safe and manageable max speed of just 2.8 mph. The single-seat version comes in six colors, while the dual-seat version offers seven.

While this ride-on Jeep replica claims to be for kids aged three to six, reviewers say that because of the roll bar it’s actually ideal for younger, smaller kids who can easily slide into the seat. Keep an eye on that weight limit.

This battery-powered ATV delivers rugged fun in a package that looks ready for the trails. Four-wheel suspension helps smooth out bumps, while Bluetooth connectivity, LED lights, and realistic ATV styling add to the excitement. Parents will love that it comes in four color choices, making it easy to match every young rider’s personality. Whether cruising the driveway or exploring the backyard, it’s built for hours of outdoor adventure.

Give your little driver a taste of supercar life with this officially licensed Lamborghini Urus ride-on. Inspired by the luxury SUV’s sleek styling, it features working LED lights, opening doors, spring suspension, realistic engine sounds, and built-in music for an immersive driving experience. Kids can take the wheel themselves or let parents guide the fun with the included remote control. Available in five eye-catching colors, it’s a stylish choice for young car enthusiasts who want to cruise in Lamborghini-inspired fashion.

If you’re wanting to give your kids the ultimate off-road adventurer, look no further than Peg Perego’s Polaris RZR PRO Green Shadow. This 24-volt ride-on features two speeds (that top out at 3.5 and 7.5 mph) as well as reverse, and it comes with enough power and suspension to get over nearly any terrain.

The Green Shadow comes with two seats with a seatbelt, as well as a storage spot in the back for your kids to carry around whatever they need to support their adventures. The rubber wheels are a step up from a lot of the ride-ons on this list and make for a quieter ride when on pavement or asphalt. Other fun features include a built-in radio, working headlights, and a start button.

We’ve been testing one over the past month and our children have loved whipping it around the backyard. Assembly can be tough, but the made-in-Italy construction is solid and should last for years and years to come. Peg Perego recommends this for children between the ages of six and 12, but our four-year-old has no problem tearing up grass in the backyard.

Featuring sirens, speakers, and flashing police lights, this Fire Chief SUV gives children the most realistic experience of driving a fire truck. It’s designed for kids aged three to six, with a maximum weight capacity of 67 pounds.

For chasing pesky bank robbers around the backyard, this ride-on police SUV is a great option. Complete with lights, sirens, a suspension system, and a push-to-talk radio speaker, it’s got just about everything a budding police officer needs.

For little speed demons with big supercar dreams, this officially licensed Lamborghini STO ride-on delivers serious wow factor. The sleek design mirrors the real exotic sports car, while a powerful 24-volt battery, drift mode, and speeds up to 6 mph make every driveway feel like a racetrack. Parents will appreciate the included remote control and safety features, while kids will love the lights, sounds, and realistic driving experience. Recommended for ages three to eight.

Adventurous kids will love this ride-on ATV. LED headlights, a kid-friendly wide seat, and a working horn create a fun and realistic ATV experience. Slow-start technology and enhanced braking make for a safe and comfortable ride. Bluetooth connectivity and a USB port let your kid crank the tunes that drive their adventures.

The Segway GoKart Pro 2 is an adrenaline-fueled go-kart that’s perfect for kids, teens, and adults seeking a high-speed thrill. It can reach speeds up to 26.7 mph and has enough acceleration to make even adults think twice before slamming on the accelerator.

With adjustable frame and steering settings, riders from four-foot-two to six-foot-two can comfortably race, drift, or explore up to 15.5 miles on a single charge. Both my children and I found the GoKart Pro 2 thrilling to ride in the time we spent testing one. The kart’s four riding modes (Eco, Sport, Race, and Manual) make it versatile for both beginner and experienced drivers, with speed caps as low as 5 mph for cautious riding.

My children appreciated the Eco mode’s manageable speed as they got comfortable, while I enjoyed the ability to switch it to Race mode to push its full potential around the neighborhood.

It’s a high-end investment but worth it considering what it offers. For added fun, the Pro 2 also has an engine-sound simulator via an included Bluetooth speaker, which connects to the go-kart to simulate the revs of different engine configurations (V-6, V-8, V-12). This go-kart is thrilling to ride and is sure to offer years of fun for drivers of all skill levels.

This 24-volt tractor is equipped with both a front loader and a detachable trailer. Kids can easily operate the front loader, making scoops, lifts, carries, and dumps from the driver’s seat (which includes a seatbelt). The powerful dual motor (with metal gears) features high and low speeds plus reverse, up to 5 mph. Max weight limit is 65 pounds.

For older kids, a little electric motorcycle might be the move. Razor makes the excellent Dirt Rocket in many variations, but the one shown here (the MX125) is geared more toward the seven-to-eight-year-old range. Though if something more exciting is of interest, Razor scales this model up in power (and age suggestion).

All feature dual suspension and riser handlebars, pneumatic knobby tires, a retractable kickstand, and hand-operated brakes. While all are undeniably cute and cool, these motocross bikes are not toys for small children.

Little land movers will feel right at home in this ride-on dump truck. It’s the ultimate fun machine. With two 35-watt motors, it features two speeds when manually controlled by the child using the foot pedal, and three speeds (top speed 3 mph) with the parent remote control. It also has a built-in Bluetooth speaker and a working dump bed. With automatic lifting and an extra shovel, kids can pitch in with the yardwork by carrying leaf piles and debris.

Little bikers will love this chopper-style “motorcycle” (that’s really a trike, so it won’t fall over). It features a working, adjustable LED headlight, pedal operation, forward/reverse, and more. The only things missing are a black t-shirt and a goatee. Designed for kids three years and up, with a weight limit of 66 pounds.

If your kid is ready to take to the not-so-open road, here’s what to look for in an electric car for kids.

While it can be tempting to get a ride-on that your child will grow into and use for years, there are safety risks involved with choosing one that’s too large or powerful for your kid to control easily.

Most electric ride-on cars feature speeds between 1.5 and 5 mph, but the more powerful you go, the higher that top speed climbs. Check the manufacturer’s recommendations for age and weight. Some even offer parental remote controls and seatbelts, while others let you remove features such as side panels as your child grows.

The biggest concern safety-wise with these toys is not so much the product itself but where the children take them. Hilly terrain can cause them to flip, and bodies of water aren’t meant to be driven through. It’s also very important to convey that these aren’t meant to be taken near a road, as their small profile can be difficult to see by drivers of normal-size vehicles.

Electric ride-ons come in multiple styles to match kids’ varying interests. Classic cars and trucks mimic real-life vehicles, offering features such as working headlights and sound effects for a realistic experience. ATVs and UTVs are built for rougher terrain with “all-terrain” tires and higher clearances. For kids who love motorcycles, bike-style ride-ons can often include training wheels for added stability.

Most electric ride-ons are powered by rechargeable batteries, typically ranging from six to 24 volts. Higher voltage generally translates to more power and a longer run time, but it’s important to match the power to the terrain and age level.

Models with 12-volt batteries provide a good balance of speed and battery life for mixed-terrain use, while 24-volt versions can handle tougher trails and inclines. Be mindful that all batteries will gradually lose capacity, so check for compatible replacement options if you plan to use the ride-on for years to come.

Interactive features can make a big difference in the overall experience. Some ride-ons include Bluetooth speakers or FM radios, letting kids listen to their favorite songs while driving. Others offer realistic details such as functional doors, working headlights and taillights, and engine sound effects.

Football Question on The Chase Had Everyone Baffled

📅 2022-09-03  |  Read Source →

Die-hard football fans would like to believe that they know everything there is to know about the sport - whether it be the history of a tournament's champions, recent transfers between teams, or the laws of the game.

The latter, in particular, is a certainty given the number of hours avid football fans have put into either attending games or watching their teams on TV.

Some laws are obvious. When a player is offside, it's usually black or white thanks to current technology. The same can be said for the majority of handballs, too, even if VAR has done its best to complicate things.

Yet, it seems that not all of football's laws are as easy to understand, as highlighted by a question that was asked on the popular British teatime game show The Chase.

Hosted by Bradley Walsh, the quiz show sees four contestants square off against a 'chaser,' who is an expert in all things general knowledge.

However, in this instance, even the accomplished Shaun Wallace found himself stumped by what may be the most difficult sports question in quiz show history.

Two Pointless contestants won the jackpot against the odds after naming Henrik Larsson as one of their answers in the final round

In a law that even those involved on the show questioned the legitimacy of, the contestant who stepped up to the plate was asked: "In football, if a direct free-kick goes straight into a team's own goal, what is awarded to the team in the opposing goal?" Watch the clip below:

While the answer may appear obvious at first, the potential answers throw a spanner in the works. The contestant, named Francesca, had the option of either a) Goal, b) Indirect free-kick, or c) Corner to choose from. But having admitted that she wasn't a football fan, she was taking a stab in the dark.

Ordinarily, this would give the chaser the perfect opportunity to close the gap needed to catch the player. However, when the camera panned to Wallace, nicknamed the 'Dark Destroyer,' he looked as baffled as anyone. The 66-year-old was open-mouthed and shook his head while whispering, "I can't remember," but the best reaction came from presenter Walsh.

After Wallace's admission, Walsh, who was a promising young player that was once on the books at Brentford, chimed in with his own thoughts on the question:

"It's not that I can't remember. I'll tell you what it is. A - a goal. B - an indirect free-kick. C - a corner. Or D - an absolute miracle. You don't need to watch football, it's never going to happen."

Admittedly, the television personality is right in that the chances of the situation happening are incredibly slim. Understandably, it would make sense to think that the correct answer would be a goal, as that would be the sufficient punishment for the mistake.

As a panic guess, Francesca opted to go for answer c) Corner, to which Walsh scoffed at her. Incredibly, though, she was right - much to the shock of everyone. It also turned out that Wallace had also guessed the correct answer, though he played it off as if he knew all along.

Due to the eyebrow-raising nature of the answer, many people wanted to find out for themselves and resorted to checking the FA handbook to see if it was true.

And yes, under Law 13: Free Kicks, IFAB's 2026-27 laws state that:

The archaic law will likely never be changed due to the fact that the chances of an own-goal being scored from a direct free-kick are so slim that it will never be argued in the future.

However, it still remains one of the strangest rules the game has ever seen, up there with the likes of the 'silver goal' or the 'advance 10m rule'.

The Difference Between A Captain & A First Officer

📅 2022-07-19  |  Read Source →

Many airlines have one of the two cockpit pilots make an announcement before takeoff, welcoming passengers and briefing them on the flight plan. Often, pilots also make subsequent announcements about the flight. Is it always the Captain making the welcoming and subsequent announcements? Or is it the first officer?

Have you ever wondered who was in the front seat of the plane you were on? Moreover, what are the differences between the duties of captains and first officers? Some people automatically assume that it is the captain doing the bulk of the work, as they are the higher-ranking pilot. However, that is not always the case. As such, we thought we would take a look at the differences between the captain and the first officer.

Long-haul flight crews in the late 1950s and 1960s consisted of the captain, first officer, relief first officer, flight engineer, navigator, and radio operator. However, as aviation advanced, planes became easier to fly with fewer people. As such, nowadays, nearly all commercial passenger flights are flown by two people: a captain and a first officer. However, longer flights will still have relief pilots onboard.

While both the captain and the first officer are licensed pilots, the former bears primary responsibility for the flight, and is the person in overall command. To recognize the captain and the first officer, look at the sleeves of their uniforms. The captain will have four stripes on their uniform, while the first officer will have three. Age and gender do not determine who the captain and the first officer are.

Generally speaking, the flight's captain will always occupy the left seat while the first officer sits on the right. We will examine the historical reasons behind this operational quirk later on. Sometimes, the captain may sit in the right seat, but it is for training and monitoring. Before each flight, the captain decides whether they will fly the aircraft or whether the first officer will be the pilot flying (PF).

Whoever is PF controls the plane, performs the takeoff, sets the autopilot, and does the landing. The pilot not flying - known as the Pilot Monitoring (PM) - fills out the flight log and communicates with air traffic control (ATC) while supporting the PF.

Usually, over the course of the working day, to divvy up the duties, the captain and the first officer take turns as the PF, flying one leg as the pilot flying and the second leg as the pilot monitoring. On longer flights, the captain and first officer may make multiple rotations, particularly on ultra-long-haul flights where a relief pilot will be involved too. Captains and first officers can use this downtime to catch up on some sleep - known as "controlled rest" - which is a common practice on long-haul operations.

During adverse weather and often at the end of the day, the captain will fly the aircraft when fatigue may start to play a role in decision-making. There are also some airports, like Funchal Airport (FNC) on the Portuguese island of Madeira, where only the captain can land because of difficulties associated with the airport.

There is a multitude of different reasons as to why the captain isn't always the pilot in command of the aircraft. To list just a few, these include:

Ultimately, the responsibility of ensuring the safety of a multi-million-dollar aircraft and its passengers rests with the captain. Because of this, they are compensated accordingly, with salaries varying depending on their level of seniority and aircraft type.

A captain at a major airline in the USA will usually start on more than $300,000 a year, rising to upwards of $450,000 annually for the most senior pilots. A first officer with a major US airline can expect a starting salary of at least $100,000, but this may rise above $250,000 for senior officers on larger aircraft.

As mentioned, airline captains generally sit in the cockpit's left-hand seat. Simple Flying explored the reasons behind this, finding that it dates back to the era of rotary-driven aircraft. The torque of these planes meant that it was easier for them to turn left, and thus, captains sat there so that they would be on the inside of the turn when flying left-turn traffic patterns.

This tendency later played a role in forming the practice of boarding airliners from the left-hand side. When aircraft used to park parallel to terminals, it made sense to keep the buildings on their left due to the captain sitting there.

Aerotime Hub highlights some criteria that allow first officers to transition to the position of captain.

Ultimately, both pilots are fully licensed and share the flying, but the captain holds overall command. That is why captains wear four stripes to the first officer’s three, sit in the left seat, and earn far more. Duties are split between pilot flying and pilot monitoring rather than by rank, and first officers can move up to captain by building hours and meeting airline requirements.

18 Best Raincoats for Men 2026, According to GQ Editors

📅 2022-04-26  |  Read Source →

Decades ago, your only options for rainy weather coverage were some kind of trench coat, a coarse wool overcoat, or, if you really needed to be out in it, a thick rubber sack that kept you dry but didn’t breathe. Thankfully, material science has advanced.

There are, of course, umbrellas? And we won’t stop you looking into those. But ask anyone from the Pacific Northwest, and they’ll tell you their rain jacket does all that work with ease. That’s because raincoats aren’t an accessory to your outfit: they’re the main focus. A good raincoat can turn your sad ensemble into head-turning Paparazzi fodder, or at the very least, keep you dry and stylish when it’s wet out.

Still not convinced? We figured—so we tested the best rain jackets and coats for men on the market right now, from the tried-and-true natural-fabric mainstays to the buzzy, newfangled riffs, and everything in between. Here they are.

Arc'teryx's Beta LT jacket is the pinnacle of no-BS rain defense, beloved by wannabe Everest climbers, GQ Recommends editors, and meme-savvy TikTokers alike. Its custom Gore-Tex fabrication will keep you from getting soaked during the harshest of downpours, while its breathable pores work overtime to let water vapor (a.k.a. sweat) escape. That sleek, streamlined silhouette also lends itself naturally to a range of pairings, from straight-fit jeans and sneakers to a full-on “Scaling Kilimanjaro” kit—cargos, backpack, hiking boots—perfect for all of your wildcard outdoor activities.

It’s an investment, but hundreds of guys were showering in theirs for a reason: If you need top-tier weather protection and long-term durability—and are willing to invest—this is still the best rain jacket for serious outdoor use. That said, most dudes chasing the clout that Arc’teryx affords won’t need to max out its capabilities. Still, it’s good to know that if you’re ever caught in a downpour that won’t let up, the Beta’s the one waterproof jacket that won’t leave you high and, uh, wet.

When it comes to outdoor gear that keeps up with Mother Nature, Patagonia’s among the first to come to mind. The OG gorpcore label has more than its fair share of bangers for every climate from the iconic Baggies shorts to its range of plush fleece jackets, and when it comes to rainy weather, there’s the Torrentshell jacket. It’s a canonical piece of kit for Patagonia and has kept customers dry and fly for years.

The latest version features a three-layer shell system that maximizes water-repellency and breathability with a 100% recycled nylon face fabric. It features toasty microfleece-lined handwarmer pockets, welted zippers for water protection (plus pit zips for ventilation), and the entire thing can pack down into itself. So pack it up, throw it in your bag, and bust it out whenever the weather turns out to be worse than what the weatherman says. With a feature set like that, you’d expect to pay through the nose, but we’re thrilled to say that it doesn’t even break $200.

The advancements in rain-wicking technology tickles our lizard brains as much as watching a rock-crushing machine turn a boulder into pebbles. But as much as we appreciate multi-layered DWR-coated materials and heat-sealed seams give us joy, we also have a great reverence and appreciation for rain coats of yore. Enter the waxed jacket, a time-tested fabric used by sailors off the British coast since the 1800s.

If you’re gonna get a waxed jacket, you’d best get a Barbour, the reigning champ of waxed jackets. Barbour has more options and collaborations than ever, so it can be tricky to get your head around what’s what but for our money, the classic Beaufort is the Goldilocks of wax jackets. Where the Bedale is shorter and styles like the Border run down to the mid-thigh, the Beaufort is just right but still long enough to layer over your sport coats. Whichever you choose, don’t forget to re-wax at home after a few seasons. Guys seem to be nervous to do it, but it’s easy, and everytime I’ve re-waxed mine, people compliment me on how great it looks. The reward for your grunt work is a jacket you'll keep for decades to come.

This season, J.Press has unearthed a Rare Barbour: the Burghley. It hasn’t been in the brand’s regular rotation for a number of years, earning it a following among collectors in places like Japan. But now it’s back in all its sweeping, full-length glory.

Originally designed to extend past the knees (and over the saddle and tops of riding boots) the Burghley protects the rider from rain and thorns. It’s a dramatic silhouette that will set you apart from all the cropped Transport and Bedales out there. Sure, it has equestrian heritage, but you needn’t be keeping a stable to wear one. It’s a great alternative to a trench, at home in the city as well as the country. And yes, it’s still made in England.

The perfect trench coat does exist, and Burberry, inventor of the style's signature gabardine fabric in 1879, cracked the code on it long ago. In the nearly 150 years since, surprisingly little has changed about the silhouette, and for good reason. The classic fit means it's roomy enough to layer over your slouchiest Armani-inspired suiting, while the belted design gives it instant sophistication. Plus, the lining and under-collar check pattern is unmistakably Burberry—an investment-worthy flex since the coat was invented.

Its WWI heritage is well-documented—British officers wore it in the trenches, using details like the shoulder flap for rifle recoil and belt rings for canteens and grenades serving real military functions. Today, it’s less about battlefield utility and more about how that water-resistant cotton gabardine will keep you dry in light city rain. I like the black, but the classic tan is always an option for you too.

Another entry from Vancouver—what can we say, they know a few things about rain up there. Indie label James Coward sources fabric from mills known for their quality and considered production practices, then makes its garments locally in its workshop. This coat is cut from the brand’s durable, waterproof ‘Mastershield cloth, a dense weave that offers protection from the elements. A generous silhouette and roomy raglan sleeves give it natural gravitas in gloomy weather, all while keeping the look relaxed and easy to layer.

Whereas the Arc’teryx Beta is the brand’s versatile all-mountain shell, the Alpha SV is built for technical climbing and severe weather. A helmet-compatible hood, harness-ready chest pockets and pit zips make it the top dog of storm shells.

HAVEN puts a GORPcore spin on the refined, city-ready trench made from three-layer GORE-TEX PRO, a more rugged fabric typically found in shells for climbing and backcountry skiing. It’s serious storm gear with a city sensibility, ready to make you feel invincible during a rainy commute.

The wrap coat is Lemaire’s runaway hit. But this Ventile-cotton style is a rainy-day flex: densely woven, breathable cotton that swells when wet to help keep wind and rain out, without synthetic fibres or coatings. Chic.

Menswear can get a little obsessive about fabric specs and provenance. But when a jacket is this cool, you get why. 100 percent Giza cotton, woven at maximum density in Saitama, Japan and originally developed for the British Air Force and later recommissioned by Japan’s Coast Guard. Yeah, that’s the good stuff.

Prep never left, but J.Press is certainly on its way back. The label’s updated take on a classic hooded parka keeps the familiar military shape sans PFAS with natural Ventile cotton. Choose classic army green, or eye-popping orange.

Haider Ackermann's take on Canada Goose is coming into focus. The brand’s Snow Goose sub-label is more Milan than Manitoba, trading logo-heavy designs for cool colours and modern silhouettes that go well beyond down parkas.

Making a good rain jacket might not take a degree in nuclear science, but Outdoor Research’s founder was actually a nuclear physicist turned avid mountaineer. This stripped-back shell sheds weight and packs small without skimping on protection. Stash it and forget it.

Marmot, meanwhile didn’t pull back on features to shave weight. This soft, quiet waterproof shell is built for movement, with an “Angel-Wing” design that lets you reach overhead without the hem riding up and putting your backside on display.

Reigning Champ has also gone well beyond sweats and tees. This workhorse of a rain jacket is more downtown than summit in style but still meets the moment with GORE-TEX construction and a very digestible price.

Italian fabric. Fifth-generation Portuguese construction. New York City design. That’s the mix behind Knickerbocker’s full-length trench. Its tightly woven, water-repellent fabric helps keep rain out all with the kind of easy, downtown cool Knickerbocker does so well.

Uniqlo’s even more affordable sister brand, GU, delivers a lot of jacket for the money The throwback piping and punchy colours nod to the ’90s, while the water- and wind-resistant fabric makes it practical, too.

A waxed Harrington probably isn’t for a downpour unless your trousers are waxed, too, but it’s ideal for breezy, drizzly, and sunny fall days alike. And, aye, the waxed fabric comes straight from Scotland. No messing about.

Who wants to drag a sopping wet umbrella around only to forget it at the restaurant or in the back of a cab? When you’ve got a trench coat with your cell and headphones in the pockets, it’s almost impossible to lose. Through light mists, heavy rain, and even torrential downpours, the best rain coats are, ironically, the drippiest too. They’ll prevent you from showing up to the function like a poor wet dog and instead make your arrival a warm, dry welcome.

Trench coats that aren’t the only coats vying to shield you from the rain, though. Gorpcore’s popularity has given us waves of tech-y jackets, parkas, and anoraks all wrought from futuristic multi-layered materials that balance breathability with waterproof ability. The result is a cementing of this 21st century sportswear into must-have menswear. And let’s not forget the workwear-adjacent waxed jackets born from sailing the Scottish seas in 15th-century Scotland. With their rugged good looks and a lust for patina, they’ve become stylish staples when the weather’s all doom and gloom.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)
